## Original problem (task)
[d31d61f36df18c74] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.response.0)
[5a43a98b0f832dd9] (h005.fork5.p.response.0)
Source account: daily/mini_fcl/cycle-1/account; selected view: both
Artifact: a1433eaa96790cf638ef36cbfe8f532da2ab32eaacec154e2c4ae5f335c71540
Original body SHA256: 6ff421b85cd28b710f310cc83e1190040aed277195b31b2ef15d68d8ff91b62f
Original commitments SHA256: 05f5b50464ada3996429ed2149ef66de7b98e12c6f7d9718384f1088a9f6eb4d
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The situation describes a breakdown in shared mental models regarding household labor. The primary friction point is not the chores themselves, but the ambiguity of verbal agreements combined with dynamic schedules. When plans change and agreements are unwritten, recollections diverge, creating a sense of unreliability. The avoidance behavior indicates that the conflict resolution process itself has become a stressor. To address this, the group should decouple task assignment from personal negotiation by implementing a visible, static system (such as a whiteboard or shared app). Re-engaging the avoiding friend requires a shift in framing: invite them to help design the system rather than to discuss past failures. This lowers the stakes and restores agency.

Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
BODY
The proposed account identifies ambiguity as the primary friction point but recommends a solution that may reintroduce negotiation burdens. Characterizing the tracking system as static conflicts with the acknowledged reality of dynamic schedules; a static board requires dynamic maintenance, which necessitates the very conversations the group seeks to streamline. Additionally, the strategy to re-engage the avoiding friend assumes avoidance stems from conflict stress rather than overwhelm or shame. Inviting them to design a system may be perceived as additional labor, potentially deepening avoidance. Finally, the account does not specify who maintains the system, risking a shift of burden onto the non-avoiding friends.
COMMITMENTS

BODY
The input account diagnoses a breakdown in shared mental models and proposes a structural fix. However, this view risks treating the symptom (ambiguity) rather than the cause (mismatched standards). Verbal agreements fail not only because they are unwritten, but because 'clean' is subjective. A static system enforces assignment without resolving definition. The avoiding friend's behavior may signal exhaustion from enforcing their standards against others, not just stress from negotiation. A rival approach suggests negotiating 'finished states' before assigning tasks. Re-engagement should invite the avoiding friend to define 'enough' rather than design the tracking system, reducing the cognitive load placed on them.
